paragraphs: This paper develops a chip that converts grayscale images into compact descriptions of their edges. These image vectors are intended to support recognition fast enough for real-time use. A central challenge is choosing the edge-detection threshold, which controls which image changes count as edges and therefore influences the features passed to recognition.

The design uses a four-stage asynchronous median-detection architecture built from a mixture of analog and digital circuits. This architecture determines the threshold and connects that calculation directly to edge-feature-map generation. The contribution is therefore an integrated processing pipeline, with threshold selection included in the hardware path that produces the image representation.

The authors fabricated a prototype using 0.35-micrometer CMOS technology and verified the concept on the chip. It produces a 64-dimensional feature vector from a 64-by-64-pixel image every 80 microseconds. The reported speed advantage over software makes real-time image recognition feasible, although the demonstrated output is the feature vector that such a recognition system would use.
neurips-2003-a-mixed-signal-vlsi-for-rea.tldr: A mixed-signal chip generates compact edge-based image vectors every 80 microseconds, supporting real-time image recognition.

paragraphs: This paper asks how closely a probability distribution can be represented by a probabilistic graphical model of manageable complexity. The central issue is a tradeoff: an approximation should retain enough of the original distribution to be accurate, while its graphical representation should remain sufficiently simple. The authors study that balance rather than treating approximation quality and model complexity as separate questions.

They introduce effective treewidth, a parameter designed to describe this accuracy-versus-complexity relationship. Its role is to characterize how well a distribution can be approximated at different levels of complexity. This gives the analysis a way to express degrees of approximability instead of reducing the question to whether a particular representation is possible.

The proposed analysis uses threshold behavior in monotone graph properties to investigate achievable tradeoffs. This connects changes in graph structure with the approximation problem. Experiments support the approach, providing empirical backing for the analysis. The stated contribution is both a new descriptive parameter and a way to reason about the compromises available when choosing a graphical approximation.
neurips-2003-approximability-of-probabil.tldr: Effective treewidth characterizes the tradeoff between accuracy and complexity when approximating distributions with graphical models.

paragraphs: Autonomous helicopter flight requires a controller to handle dynamics that are both complex and noisy. This paper describes a successful application of reinforcement learning to that control problem. The tasks include maintaining a stationary hover and carrying out several maneuvers drawn from a radio-controlled helicopter competition, covering both holding position and executing movement.

The approach begins by fitting a model of the helicopter's dynamics. That model is nonlinear, allowing it to represent behavior beyond a simple linear relationship, and stochastic, incorporating uncertainty into its description. The learned dynamics model then becomes the basis for learning flight control. This connects estimating how the helicopter behaves with finding how to control it.

The reported outcome is successful learning for hovering and the selected competition maneuvers. The significance is the application of reinforcement learning to a physical control setting where uncertainty and nonlinear behavior are central to the problem. The paper's sequence of modeling and control learning provides a concrete route from a description of helicopter dynamics to autonomous flight behavior.
neurips-2003-autonomous-helicopter-fligh.tldr: A learned stochastic, nonlinear dynamics model enables reinforcement learning for autonomous helicopter hovering and competition maneuvers.

paragraphs: Knowing which neurons connect does not by itself explain how a nervous system produces behavior. This paper addresses that gap in C. elegans by studying chemotaxis, in which the animal's probability of turning changes with the rate of change of chemical concentration. The computational question is how a neural circuit can convert this sensory history into a behavioral response.

The authors use optimization to search for connection patterns sufficient to perform that transformation. The search produces differentiator networks: circuits that respond to changes in the chemical signal. These networks include inhibitory feedback among all neurons. Further analysis shows that feedback regulates the delay between sensory input and the resulting behavior, giving those connections a role in response timing.

Some connection patterns in the optimized models resemble patterns in the biological nervous system. These similarities suggest possible functions for previously identified connections. The result supplies circuit-level hypotheses grounded in a required computation; it establishes sufficient model arrangements and proposes biological interpretations, without establishing that the animal must use precisely those arrangements.
neurips-2003-circuit-optimization-predic.tldr: Optimized circuits suggest that inhibitory feedback can support chemical-change detection and regulate behavioral response timing in C. elegans.

paragraphs: Generative and discriminative classifiers can have different advantages depending on how much labeled data is available. The paper starts from evidence that discriminative training usually works better with abundant labels, while generative classifiers can perform better when training data is limited. It proposes combining the two training approaches within a single classification model.

The hybrid divides its parameters into two groups. A large, high-dimensional group is fitted by maximizing generative likelihood, while a small group is fitted by maximizing conditional likelihood. This reserves discriminative training for a restricted part of the model. A sample-complexity bound shows that fitting these discriminative parameters well requires a number of examples that depends only logarithmically on feature occurrences and feature-set size.

Experiments show that the hybrids can achieve lower test error and better accuracy-versus-coverage curves than either purely generative or purely discriminative counterparts. These results support the proposed division of training responsibilities. The theoretical bound concerns the discriminative parameter subset, while the empirical results establish that combining objectives can benefit classification in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2003-classification-with-hybrid-.tldr: Training most parameters generatively and a small subset discriminatively can improve classification while limiting the discriminative training data requirement.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to draw samples from a distribution formed by multiplying several Gaussian mixtures. That operation appears in nonparametric belief propagation and in training product-of-experts models. The authors develop two multiscale sampling algorithms, addressing a computational task shared by these different modeling settings.

The first algorithm adapts previously proposed Monte Carlo techniques to a multiscale approach. It retains comparable theoretical guarantees while showing faster empirical convergence. The second uses approximate kernel-density evaluation to build a fast approximate sampler. Its guarantee is controlled by a tunable epsilon: sampled points have probabilities within that tolerance of their true probabilities. The two methods therefore offer different combinations of sampling strategy and approximation control.

Both algorithms are evaluated on computational examples motivated by nonparametric belief propagation, where they show significant improvements over existing methods. The findings distinguish empirical speed gains from the guarantees attached to each algorithm. Together, the methods provide more efficient ways to perform mixture-product sampling, with the second explicitly exposing an adjustable accuracy tolerance.
neurips-2003-efficient-multiscale-sampli.tldr: Two multiscale algorithms improve sampling from products of Gaussian mixtures, with theoretical guarantees and demonstrated computational gains.

paragraphs: The eye continues to move slightly even during steady fixation. A dynamic theory of vision proposes that these movements can improve fine visual discrimination by shifting spatial excitation across photoreceptors. Later processing could combine the resulting patterns across space and time. This paper reexamines that proposal with a realistic model of the vertebrate retina.

The authors compare a resting eye with a moving eye and evaluate simulated ganglion-cell responses in a hyperacuity task. Ideal-observer analysis assesses how much task-relevant information those responses provide. This makes the comparison about the usefulness of the retinal signals for discrimination, rather than simply whether movement changes the signals.

The results depend on retinal location. In the central retina, micro-movements do not improve performance because optical blur limits vernier acuity in the model. In the peripheral retina, they clearly improve performance. ROC analysis yields quantitative predictions that could be tested electrophysiologically and psychophysically. The findings therefore support a location-dependent benefit in simulation and specify a route to experimental testing.
neurips-2003-eye-micro-movements-improve.tldr: Retinal simulations predict that tiny eye movements improve peripheral hyperacuity but provide no central benefit where optical blur limits performance.

paragraphs: Microarray classification seeks accurate decision rules that depend on only a small number of genes. This paper develops feature-selection algorithms for linear threshold functions with that objective in mind. Selecting genes is part of building a compact classifier, so the method must balance predictive usefulness with reducing how many features the rule uses.

The algorithms combine backward elimination with adaptive regularization. Features are removed through the elimination process, while regularization adapts as part of the procedure. An incremental large-margin algorithm supplies the computational core. The authors describe the resulting methods as fast and straightforward to implement because they avoid linear, quadratic, and higher-order programming methods.

Preliminary experiments use five established DNA microarray datasets. Their results suggest that multiplicative large-margin algorithms tend to outperform additive algorithms, including SVMs, on feature-selection tasks. The finding is a qualified empirical tendency from those experiments. It supports further interest in multiplicative updates when the goal is an accurate classifier using few genes, alongside the proposed method's computational simplicity.
neurips-2003-fast-feature-selection-from.tldr: Fast feature-selection methods combine backward elimination and adaptive regularization, with preliminary microarray results favoring multiplicative large-margin algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper combines finding groups in data with selecting the features used to define those groups. Its approach is a wrapper strategy: features are evaluated through the partitioning algorithm itself. The selection objective directly reflects that algorithm's ability to distinguish the resulting groups, tying the chosen representation to the clustering procedure.

The authors provide an efficient optimization algorithm with a guarantee of local convergence. This gives the procedure a stated convergence property without asserting that it always reaches the globally best solution. The method has one free parameter, which is selected using a resampling-based stability analysis. Repeatedly reconsidering the data through resampling supplies the basis for this parameter choice.

Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that the method can recover both meaningful partitions and meaningful feature subsets. Those are complementary outputs: one describes how observations group together, and the other identifies which variables support the grouping. The contribution is an integrated way to obtain both, with feature selection guided by the clustering algorithm and parameter selection guided by stability.
neurips-2003-feature-selection-in-cluste.tldr: A clustering wrapper selects useful features directly, with locally convergent optimization and stability-based tuning.

paragraphs: Why does a sequence look random to a person, and when does it appear to contain a pattern? This paper treats that judgment as a model-selection problem. Given a stimulus, the observer is understood as inferring whether a random process or a regular process generated it. This frames perceived randomness as a question about competing explanations.

Inspired by Kolmogorov complexity, the authors describe regularity using a hierarchy of automata. Each combines a finite controller with a particular form of memory. The hierarchy provides different capacities for identifying structure in a sequence, connecting the patterns a mechanism can recognize with the memory resources available to it.

The study finds that the regularities people detect in binary sequences depend on how the sequences are presented. Automata capable of identifying those regularities are informative about the cognitive processes involved in different presentation formats. The result links subjective randomness to both stimulus structure and the processes used to inspect it: the same general task can engage different ways of recognizing regularity.
neurips-2003-from-algorithmic-to-subject.tldr: A model-selection account links perceived randomness to the memory mechanisms and presentation formats involved in detecting patterns.

paragraphs: Gene-expression time courses can differ in both their shapes and their timing. This paper proposes a functional mixture model that groups these curves while aligning them in time. Although measurements occur on a discrete time grid, the model describes cluster centers with continuous-time functions, allowing it to estimate shifts that are not restricted to whole sampling intervals.

Each cluster center is a nonlinear combination of solutions to a simple linear differential equation describing mRNA change under constant synthesis and decay rates. These functional building blocks connect the curve representation to mRNA production and loss. The mixture accommodates different profile types, while smooth mean curves regularize noisy measurements.

The authors derive an expectation-maximization algorithm for estimating the model and apply it to cycling genes in yeast. Experiments show consistent improvements in predictive power and within-cluster variance compared with ordinary Gaussian mixtures. The findings support modeling expression profiles as temporally adjustable curves: the grouping can reflect shared dynamics even when those dynamics occur at different times.
neurips-2003-gene-expression-clustering-.tldr: A continuous-time mixture model jointly clusters and aligns gene-expression curves, improving predictions and cluster consistency on cycling yeast genes.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates an energy-normalization transform for reducing errors in the LF-ASD brain-computer interface. The system distinguishes active EEG data from idle EEG data, making the separation between these classes important to its performance. The proposed transform changes how signal energy enters that distinction.

The authors identify two potential benefits. Normalization can make active and idle data more separable, and it can reduce sensitivity to variations in signal amplitude. These address different aspects of the classification problem: how distinct the target classes appear and how much changing signal magnitude affects the system. The transform is evaluated through its effect on the interface's performance.

Four subjects show reported performance improvements ranging from 7.7% to 18.9%. A fifth subject, whose accuracy before normalization was already the highest at 90.5%, shows no notable change. The results support normalization as a useful modification for several participants in the study, while also showing that its benefit was not uniform across all five subjects.
neurips-2003-impact-of-an-energy-normali.tldr: Energy normalization improved LF-ASD brain-computer interface performance for four of five subjects, with little change for the strongest initial performer.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the problem of maximizing information transmitted through a noisy channel. Mutual information supplies the objective, expressing how informative the channel's output is about its input. Computing that quantity is generally difficult, creating a practical obstacle to optimizing a channel or representation for information transmission.

The authors use a variational approximation to tackle this computational difficulty. The resulting information-maximization algorithm is analogous to expectation-maximization, but it targets mutual information rather than likelihood. That distinction matters because the optimization goal is the information preserved through the noisy channel, rather than how well a model assigns likelihood to observations.

The method is applied to several practical examples, including linear compression, population encoding, and CDMA. These applications place the same information-based optimization approach in different settings involving representation or transmission. The paper's contribution is a computational route to a difficult objective, together with examples of its use. Its stated scope is the variational method and these applications, rather than a quantified claim of improvement across them.
neurips-2003-information-maximization-in.tldr: A variational algorithm analogous to EM targets mutual information for optimizing transmission through noisy channels.

paragraphs: This paper compares human visual judgments with machine-learning classifiers to investigate how people classify faces. Human participants perform a gender-classification task using frontal face views. The researchers record their judgments, reaction times, and confidence ratings, giving several measures of how each face is processed.

Several algorithms learn separating hyperplanes using principal components of face texture and shape representations. Their performance is evaluated using both the database's gender labels and the labels supplied by participants. The authors then relate human responses to each face's distance from the learned decision boundary. This connects classifier geometry with behavioral measures of the human decision process.

The results suggest that some hyperplane algorithms, operating in the chosen feature space, can model human classification. Faces near the separating boundary require more processing than faces farther away. The finding gives boundary distance an interpretation beyond the predicted label: it relates to the effort involved in deciding. The support remains specific to some algorithms and the representation used in this task.
neurips-2003-insights-from-machine-learn.tldr: Human face-classification responses suggest that some learned decision boundaries capture both judgments and increased processing near ambiguous boundaries.

paragraphs: Known transformations can help a classifier recognize that altered versions of a pattern should receive the same label. This paper develops a semidefinite-programming framework for incorporating such knowledge into linear classification. Its Semidefinite Programming Machine represents training examples as polynomial trajectories, allowing a transformed pattern to be considered along a path rather than only at an individual point.

The algorithm finds a maximum-margin separating hyperplane for these trajectories. Its solution is sparse in the dual variables, and points with the smallest real-valued classifier output along a trajectory can be identified as virtual support vectors. These points reveal where the transformed examples most constrain the classifier's separation.

The authors also discuss trajectory segments, multiple transformation parameters, and kernel-based extensions. In experiments, a Taylor expansion locally approximates rotational invariance in USPS pixel images, producing improvements over known methods. The demonstrated invariance is therefore based on a local approximation. The broader contribution is a way to incorporate continuous transformation paths directly into margin-based learning.
neurips-2003-invariant-pattern-recogniti.tldr: Semidefinite Programming Machines learn maximum-margin classifiers over polynomial transformation paths, improving locally rotation-invariant image classification in experiments.

paragraphs: Kernel learning methods express their solutions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, where input patterns have been mapped into a feature representation. Some applications also need a corresponding pattern back in the original input space. This reconstruction problem is called finding a pre-image, and it is the focus of the paper.

The authors introduce a technique that combines kernel principal component analysis with regression to reconstruct input-space patterns. The approach makes reconstruction a learning problem. It avoids difficult or unstable numerical optimization and is described as easy to implement, addressing practical obstacles that can arise when trying to recover an input from a feature-space result.

A distinctive capability is computing pre-images in discrete input spaces, which the authors contrast with previous methods. This extends where the reconstruction technique can be used. The paper reviews its performance across several applications requiring pre-images. Its contribution is thus a practical connection between kernel-space solutions and usable input-space patterns, including settings where inputs take discrete values.
neurips-2003-learning-to-find-pre-images.tldr: Kernel PCA and regression provide a practical way to reconstruct input patterns from kernel features, including in discrete input spaces.

paragraphs: Automated ECG interval analysis requires separating an electrocardiogram into its constituent waveform features. This paper examines hidden Markov models and hidden semi-Markov models for that segmentation task. The modeling problem includes both identifying the sequence of features and representing how long each feature lasts.

Before modeling, the authors apply an undecimated wavelet transform to the signal. This produces an overcomplete representation that they describe as more appropriate for the subsequent models. The signal representation and the temporal model therefore address complementary parts of the task: expressing the waveform for analysis and describing how its components unfold over time.

The paper shows that the durations implicit in a standard hidden Markov model are poorly suited to real ECG features. It consequently investigates hidden semi-Markov models for improved duration modeling. This identifies a specific mismatch between the standard model and the signal's temporal structure. The contribution is the diagnosis of that mismatch and an examination of a model designed to handle feature duration more appropriately.
neurips-2003-markov-models-for-automated.tldr: ECG segmentation reveals a mismatch in standard hidden Markov duration assumptions, motivating hidden semi-Markov models.

paragraphs: Transcranial magnetic stimulation delivers a brief magnetic pulse through a coil on the scalp and can interfere with specific cortical functions with high temporal precision. This makes it useful for neuroscience experiments. The paper addresses a mechanistic question behind that use: what neural processes produce the interference caused by the pulse?

The authors propose neural mechanisms and examine them computationally. Their central comparison concerns the level of explanation: an isolated neuron versus interactions within a neural population. The reported computational evidence assigns a critical role to inhibitory interactions among neurons in producing TMS-induced interference.

This finding directs attention to how the stimulated population interacts, rather than explaining the effect solely through the response of one neuron. Its significance is a proposed theoretical basis connecting a magnetic perturbation to disruption of cortical function. The evidence is computational, so the result supports a network mechanism within that investigation; it does not by itself establish that the proposed interactions exhaust the biological mechanisms of TMS.
neurips-2003-mechanism-of-neural-interfe.tldr: Computational evidence suggests that inhibitory interactions within neural populations are critical to TMS-induced interference.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a method for describing data on a lower-dimensional manifold using an information-theoretic objective. The dimensionality reduction is nonlinear and nonparametric. Its foundation is the infinite-cluster limit of rate-distortion theory, which frames representation as a tradeoff between the information retained and the distortion introduced.

The method constrains how much information is available to the manifold coordinates. Under that constraint, a probabilistic mapping emerges from the original data to points on the lower-dimensional manifold. The mapping is therefore part of the optimized description, and assignments to the manifold are expressed probabilistically.

The information-distortion tradeoff is the method's only parameter. Within that formulation, the method determines the manifold's shape and dimensionality, the probabilistic map, and the prior that together give an optimal description of the data. The significance is that these choices are coupled by one objective. Optimality refers to this information-theoretic description, tying the chosen representation to an explicit balance between information and distortion.
neurips-2003-optimal-manifold-representa.tldr: An information-distortion objective jointly determines a nonlinear manifold, its dimensionality, and a probabilistic mapping of data onto it.

paragraphs: A speaker can be distinctive in how they use language as well as in how their voice sounds. This paper focuses on longer-term patterns of phone sequences for speaker recognition. Large speech corpora make it possible to study these patterns statistically and use them to model individual speakers.

The approach combines support vector machines with term-frequency analysis of phone sequences, borrowing techniques from text categorization. Instead of treating the recording only as an acoustic signal, it uses counts of phonetic patterns as evidence about the speaker. The authors also derive a new kernel by linearizing likelihood-ratio scoring, connecting the classifier to a scoring approach used for recognition.

The resulting phone-based SVM approach halves the error rate of conventional phone-based approaches in the reported comparison. This is a substantial stated improvement within that category of speaker-recognition methods. The result supports the usefulness of characteristic phonetic sequence usage and shows how methods for classifying text can be adapted to identity information contained in speech patterns.
neurips-2003-phonetic-speaker-recognitio.tldr: Support vector machines using phone-sequence frequencies halve the reported error rate of conventional phone-based speaker recognition.

paragraphs: Plasticity kernels describe how the timing difference between activity before and after a synapse relates to the direction and magnitude of changes in synaptic strength. This paper investigates why experimentally observed kernels have their particular forms. It develops the idea that a kernel reflects filtering intended to remove noise that would otherwise corrupt learning.

Earlier applications of this filtering interpretation concerned trace learning rules. Here, the authors apply it to experimentally defined kernels and work backward to infer assumed signal statistics. The kernel becomes evidence about the statistical environment that would make a given filtering rule appropriate, rather than only a description of how synaptic changes depend on timing.

The paper also adds a second filtering goal: weighting learning according to statistical surprise, as in a Z-score transform. This extension can change the signal statistics inferred from a kernel and can make them more natural. The contribution is an interpretive framework linking observed timing-dependent plasticity to assumptions about noise, signal structure, and how unexpected an event is.
neurips-2003-plasticity-kernels-and-temp.tldr: Interpreting plasticity kernels as noise and surprise filters allows researchers to infer the signal statistics that could underlie them.

paragraphs: Learning a motor skill involves uncertainty from both sensory measurements and the task itself. Previous experience can help by providing information about which task conditions are more likely. This paper investigates whether people represent both kinds of uncertainty and combine them when learning a new sensorimotor task.

The researchers impose a distribution on the task and manipulate variability in sensory feedback. This separates the statistics of prior task experience from the reliability of current sensory information. Subjects show evidence of internally representing both and combining them in a way qualitatively predicted by optimal Bayesian processing. The claim is qualitative agreement with that prediction, rather than exact numerical optimality.

The study also examines multimodal task distributions, including Gaussian mixtures, where prior experience contains multiple concentrations of probability. Results indicate that probabilistic modeling in sensorimotor learning extends to these more structured priors. This matters because the represented task knowledge need not collapse to one typical condition; it can reflect several distinct possibilities while being combined with uncertain feedback.
neurips-2003-probabilistic-inference-in-.tldr: People combine learned task distributions with sensory uncertainty in qualitative agreement with Bayesian processing, even for multimodal priors.

paragraphs: This paper develops sparse matrix factorization and applies it to blind source separation in the overcomplete case. The method first estimates an overcomplete basis using K-means, then obtains coefficients through minimum-l1-norm optimization. The authors prove that, for the estimated basis, this solution is unique with probability one and can be found using linear programming.

They also compare minimum-l1 and minimum-l0 solutions to support analysis of source recoverability. The uniqueness result and the comparison play different roles: a uniquely determined optimization solution still needs to be related to the source-recovery problem. When sources are insufficiently sparse, the approach uses wavelet-packet preprocessing and performs separation in the time-frequency domain.

An EEG example illustrates the method's use. The authors select two almost independent components recovered by sparse representation and examine their phase synchronization. They find periods of significant synchronization associated with tasks. This connects the factorization procedure to analysis of relationships between recovered signals, alongside the theoretical work on uniqueness and recoverability.
neurips-2003-sparse-representation-and-i.tldr: Sparse factorization combines a K-means basis with l1 optimization for overcomplete source separation and illustrates task-related synchronization in EEG components.

paragraphs: This paper presents a system for rapidly locating a single dipole source from noisy MEG measurements. A multilayer perceptron maps sensor signals and head position to a source location. Including head position addresses the previous need to retrain the network for each subject and recording session.

Training examples are generated by passing randomly selected dipoles and head positions through an analytic model, then adding noise from real MEG recordings. After training, the network produces a location in 0.7 milliseconds with an average error of 0.90 centimeters. This provides a fast initial estimate using both the measured signals and the head's position.

A few Levenberg-Marquardt iterations initialized with the network estimate take 15 milliseconds and reduce the error to 0.53 centimeters, slightly above the noise-imposed statistical accuracy limit. The authors also apply the methods to single-dipole MEG components isolated by blind source separation and compare locations with manually assisted commercial software. The approach offers rapid direct localization and a more accurate refinement option within the single-dipole setting.
neurips-2003-subject-independent-magneto.tldr: A neural network incorporating head position localizes single MEG dipoles rapidly across subjects, with iterative refinement improving accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper presents a general method for improving estimates of correlations within variational Bayes. Correlations describe relationships between quantities, so estimating them concerns more than describing each quantity individually. The focus is on improving this aspect of an approximate probabilistic description within an existing inference framework.

The proposed tool is linear response. The authors use it to derive improved correlation estimates and discuss it as a broader principle for improving mean-field approximations. This connects a particular target, the estimated relationships between quantities, with a general strategy for refining approximate inference. The contribution is presented as a method within variational Bayes rather than as an application-specific model.

Three applications illustrate the method. They provide concrete uses of the proposed framework while the broader discussion considers how linear response can guide improvements to mean-field approximations. The paper's stated contribution is therefore both methodological and illustrative: it supplies a general route to better correlation estimates and demonstrates its use in several applications.
neurips-2003-variational-linear-response.tldr: Linear response provides a general method for improving correlation estimates in variational Bayes and refining mean-field approximations.
